name: Lattice corneal dystrophy
aliases: gelsolin amyloidosis (lattice type II / Meretoja syndrome)

reference.source: Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology / Cornea by Krachmer
clinicalPearls: A stromal dystrophy characterised by branching refractile lattice lines representing amyloid deposition, best seen on slit-lamp retroillumination
The common form (type I) is autosomal dominant and caused by mutations in the TGFBI gene on chromosome 5q31, part of the TGFBI dystrophy cluster
Amyloid deposits stain with Congo red and show apple-green birefringence and dichroism under polarised light
Recurrent corneal erosions are frequent early in the disease and can dominate the symptomatic picture before vision declines
Progressive stromal haze between the lattice lines eventually reduces vision as deposits coalesce over decades

Type II lattice dystrophy (Meretoja syndrome) is a systemic gelsolin amyloidosis with cranial and peripheral neuropathy, facial mask-like features, and cutis laxa in addition to sparse corneal lattice lines
Management is largely supportive with lubrication and treatment of erosions, with phototherapeutic keratectomy or lamellar/penetrating keratoplasty for advanced visual loss
Recurrence of deposits within a corneal graft over time is characteristic and should be anticipated when counselling
reference.pathophysiology: Lattice corneal dystrophy results from the abnormal deposition of amyloid within the corneal stroma. In the classic autosomal dominant form, mutations in the transforming growth factor beta-induced gene (TGFBI) produce an abnormal protein that misfolds and aggregates as amyloid fibrils, forming the branching lattice lines and intervening haze. In the systemic type II variant (Meretoja syndrome), mutations in the gelsolin gene lead to widespread amyloid deposition affecting the cornea, cranial and peripheral nerves, and skin. Amyloid accumulation progressively disrupts stromal transparency and undermines epithelial adhesion, producing recurrent erosions and gradual loss of vision.
additionalDifferentials: Granular corneal dystrophy and combined granular-lattice (Avellino) dystrophy
Amyloid deposition secondary to chronic ocular surface disease (polymorphic amyloid degeneration)
Recurrent corneal erosion syndrome from other basement membrane dystrophy
Reis-Bucklers and Thiel-Behnke anterior stromal dystrophies
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy with retroillumination to identify branching lattice lines
Histology of corneal tissue with Congo red staining showing apple-green birefringence
Genetic testing for TGFBI mutations to confirm type and distinguish from gelsolin type II
Anterior segment optical coherence tomography to map depth of deposits
Systemic evaluation for neuropathy and skin changes when Meretoja syndrome is suspected
Corneal topography to assess irregular astigmatism before surgical planning
redFlags: Rapidly progressive visual loss suggesting dense confluent stromal amyloid
Systemic features of cranial or peripheral neuropathy indicating gelsolin type II amyloidosis
Severe or non-healing epithelial defects raising concern for secondary infection
Recurrence of deposits in a corneal graft threatening the visual result
reference.prognosis: Vision typically declines slowly over decades, with recurrent erosions often preceding visual loss. Keratoplasty can restore clarity but amyloid deposits frequently recur in the graft, and the systemic type II form carries additional neurological morbidity.
pitfalls: Attributing recurrent erosions to trauma or dry eye and missing the underlying dystrophy
Failing to recognise systemic features that point to Meretoja gelsolin amyloidosis
Not counselling patients about the near-inevitable recurrence of deposits after grafting
Overlooking the shared TGFBI origin with granular dystrophy when interpreting mixed phenotypes
references: Cornea by Krachmer, Mannis and Holland
